Chapter 2: The Trap of Making Excuses and the Cost to Self-Respect
So, now that we’ve uncovered the basic truth about genuine interest, let’s take a look at a challenge so many of us face: making excuses for someone else’s lack of effort.
It’s perfectly human, isn’t it? None of us want to feel rejected—or admit that maybe, just maybe, we care more about the relationship than the other person does. Excuses become a kind of armor, keeping disappointment at bay. But here’s the thing: that armor can also block us from real growth and meaningful connection.
Excuses come in all shapes and sizes. Maybe you’ve heard yourself say, “He’s just really busy with work,” or, “She’s probably just shy and doesn’t know how to show it.” Sometimes, the stories get more complicated—maybe there’s talk of past trauma or difficult life circumstances.
And don’t get me wrong—empathy matters. It’s important to understand where someone’s coming from. But there’s a line between being compassionate and letting someone’s struggles excuse ongoing neglect or indifference.
The real cost here? It’s often your own self-respect. Every time you accept less than you honestly need, you quietly tell yourself that your feelings and needs come second. Over weeks or months, that message sinks in, and suddenly, you might start to feel powerless—or even resentful, toward them and yourself.
I want you to picture a job interview for a second. If a company kept canceling meetings, ignoring your emails, or acting disinterested, you probably wouldn’t make excuses for them. Most people would simply move on. But when it comes to romance, those same red flags somehow get explained away. Why is that? It usually comes down to hope—and how much you’ve already invested emotionally.
Breaking free from this cycle takes some real honesty with yourself. It’s about asking those tough questions: Is this relationship giving you the basics—like respect, affection, and reliability? Are you making excuses that are truly fair, or are they just a way to avoid the truth?
This isn’t about blaming anyone. It’s about reclaiming your own sense of agency and dignity.
Here are a few gentle reminders that can help as you shift your perspective:
First, pay attention to patterns—not just isolated moments. Second, trust those feelings of disappointment or frustration; they’re telling you something important. Third, remember that you deserve to be with someone who’s genuinely excited to be with you. And finally, recognize that making excuses for someone’s lack of effort won’t bring you closer—it just keeps you stuck in uncertainty.
When you let go of excuses, you make room for relationships that are truly mutual, respectful, and fulfilling. And that’s not giving up. That’s choosing yourself—and your well-being.
